transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-07-21
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Evan Zhou (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (DataForge Head of ML), Tom Rivera (DataForge SRE), Liam O'Connor (Product)

AI Summary (auto): Demo of Redwood edge behaviors under long-context and high TPS loads. Covered runtime kernel selection, KV cache, streaming resilience, timeouts and retry semantics, and Dedicated/VPC deployment options. Customer interested in a POC and long-context benchmarks.

[00:00] Maya Patel: hey everyone thanks for joining, we're gonna walk through some of the edge case scenarios you flagged in the form, mainly long context, very high TPS, and streaming backpressure. Evan's gonna drive the technical parts, i'll cover pricing and next steps.
[00:18] Aisha Khan: great thanks, our major concern is how the model performs with 50k-100k token contexts — we have retrieval-augmented generations where the context can blow up and also, uh, live ingestion for user chat history.
[00:30] Evan Zhou: yeah totally, so first slide is architecture overview, uh, the runtime keeps a kv cache per session so we avoid recomputing tokens, and we have prefix caching for common prompts, that tends to cut down per-token work. note though that for 100k tokens you hit memory and kernel selection thresholds, so we either shard the attention or swap to long-context kernels — there can be latency spikes during that transition.
[01:05] Tom Rivera: does that mean we see tail latency jumps when we cross the kernel boundary? we run probes at 200 qps and we had a few 2-3s spikes.
[01:15] Evan Zhou: yes, you can see transient tail increases. we recommend warmup traffic and a canary that ramps through the sequence length distribution; also our autoscaler can pre-spin Dedicated workers if we detect sustained long-context patterns.
[01:35] Liam O'Connor: quick question on cost — is Dedicated the only way to avoid noisy neighbor issues at high qps?
[01:42] Maya Patel: not only, but Dedicated gives predictable throughput and you can get reserved capacity pricing; hosted can work with burst and QoS routing but if you need hard SLAs we usually recommend Dedicated + reserved commit.
[01:58] Evan Zhou: for hosted, we also have routing policies to move requests to cheaper variants when load is high, but that can affect quality. for your use case if quality must be preserved, pinned model versions on Dedicated are safer.
[02:15] Aisha Khan: you mentioned streaming backpressure — we saw clients time out when many concurrent streams are open and the network had pauses. how does Redwood handle client-side timeouts and server-side queueing?
[02:28] Evan Zhou: good one. we implement continuous streaming with a small server-side send buffer plus per-connection flow control; when the client is slow we will apply backpressure and batch other requests if possible. if the buffer fills we surface a 503 or a retryable error depending on the route policy. you can configure per-route queue limits and client read timeouts in the console.
[02:55] Tom Rivera: is that exposed in the SDK or only in the console? curious about programmatic controls.
[03:02] Evan Zhou: both — SDKs expose streaming parameters and client backoff hooks; console gives you defaults and live metrics. we'll share the SDK snippet after the call.
[03:18] [00:03:18] Aisha Khan: do you support chunked responses for really large outputs or do you require the model to stream full tokens? sometimes our UX demands partial summaries before full ranking.
[03:30] Evan Zhou: we do chunked streaming and structured output patterns; you can emit interim summaries via function calling or partial JSON. note though that chunking can increase overhead if you have thousands of concurrent small streams.
[03:48] [00:03:48] Liam O'Connor: on timeouts — what's your recommendation for client read timeouts vs server-side timeouts?
[03:55] Evan Zhou: set client read timeout slightly higher than expected generation time and use keepalive pings; server-side we have a hard request timeout that can be tuned per-route, and we recommend retry policies for idempotent calls. also for long-context runs, increase token limits and request-level timeouts.
[04:18] [00:04:18] Maya Patel: wanted to touch on observability — the console will show per-route token breakdowns, latency percentiles and kv cache hit rates. we can instrument a tracing hook into your app to correlate spikes with sequence length.
[04:36] Tom Rivera: do you keep audit logs with customer-owned keys or are logs in your control plane? security is a big blocker for our procurement.
[04:45] Evan Zhou: for Hosted logs are retained in our control plane but encrypted; for Private (VPC/on-prem) you can host the control plane in your network and point logs to your SIEM. we support KMS integrations for key separation. we'll share SOC2 and VPC deployment guide.
[05:05] [00:05:05] Aisha Khan: can you run a test POC where we feed a 100k token doc and then query different window offsets to see kv cache hits and whether the runtime prunes older KV entries?
[05:15] Evan Zhou: absolutely. the plan we usually run: 1) synthetic test with full 100k sequences at variable offsets, 2) sustained TPS ramp to simulate production patterns, 3) streaming client churn with intermittent slow clients to exercise backpressure. we have a benchmark harness we can provide.
[05:36] [00:05:36] Maya Patel: note: we'll need sample data and redaction rules from you for the POC.
[05:42] Aisha Khan: yes we'll share a sanitized dataset, maybe 10-20 large docs.
[05:48] [00:05:48] Liam O'Connor: curious about autoscale delays — if we ramp from 100 to 5k TPS quickly, how do you avoid dropping in-flight requests?
[05:57] Evan Zhou: autoscaler has a warm pool and burst capacity for Dedicated customers; for Hosted we have elastic nodes but we recommend pre-warming for big jumps. we also have graceful degradation policies to route to lower-capacity but compatible model variants rather than fail.
[06:16] [00:06:16] Tom Rivera: during one of our tests we saw streaming timeouts where the server returned partial data and then closed the connection; is that expected?
[06:24] Evan Zhou: if the runtime hits a memory limit or kernel swap we may cut a connection to avoid noisy neighbor impact; that's rare but we can surface a retryable 5xx and optionally the partial payload. for customers who need zero partial drop we run in Dedicated with higher memory configurations.
[06:45] [00:06:45] Maya Patel: pricing note — Dedicated with reserved commit and burst lanes is the typical recommendation; i'll attach a sample pricing sheet.
[06:55] Aisha Khan: on the SOC2 question, can you provide architecture docs for your control plane interaction? procurement will need them.
[07:02] Maya Patel: yes, we'll send the SOC2 summary and a network diagram for VPC Private deployment.
[07:08] [00:07:08] Evan Zhou: technical detail on long-context kernels: we choose between tiled attention, linearized attention and an out-of-core execution depending on seq len and hardware. we surface an estimated latency delta in the console's model profile so you can see when transitions might occur.
[07:30] Liam O'Connor: does that estimate account for KV cache warmup?
[07:34] Evan Zhou: we estimate cold and warm latencies separately; cold is first N tokens before cache hit rate stabilizes.
[07:45] [00:07:45] Tom Rivera: we have regulatory constraints to keep data in eu-west. how do you handle regional model serving?
[07:53] Evan Zhou: you can pin region routing in the policies; Dedicated/VPC can be provisioned in the region you choose and logs stay in-region for Private setups.
[08:08] [00:08:08] Aisha Khan: let's talk numbers — what TPS can you sustain for 4k context vs 100k?
[08:15] Evan Zhou: approximate: on a c5-ish GPU, 4k contexts we can saturate hundreds to low thousands qps depending on batch config; at 100k contexts throughput drops dramatically to tens qps per GPU unless you shard or use model partitioning and higher memory instances. exact numbers depend on model size and quantization. we'll run a 2-step benchmark for you.
[08:40] [00:08:40] Maya Patel: i'll share the benchmark spreadsheet that maps sequence length to expected qps per instance type.
[08:48] [00:08:48] Liam O'Connor: about streaming client SDKs — we need language support for our rust service. is there a rust SDK?
[08:55] Evan Zhou: we have official python and node SDKs, community rust bindings and a grpc interface that you can use from rust. we also provide example code.
[09:06] [00:09:06] Tom Rivera: any guidance for retry backoff for streaming vs unary?
[09:12] Evan Zhou: streaming retries are trickier — we recommend idempotent partial checkpointing and exponential backoff with jitter; for unary use standard retryable codes. we'll share patterns.
[09:28] [00:09:28] Maya Patel: ok let's do a short live demo — Evan, can you kick off the long-context playback?
[09:35] Evan Zhou: launching the demo now, you'll see a run where we feed a 60k token doc and then issue a sliding-window query every 10k tokens, watch the kv cache hit rate and latency percentiles on the console.
[09:50] [00:09:50] [demo audio/noise] Evan Zhou: alright so the console shows initial cold latency 820ms, warm median 120ms, and a tail spike at the kernel transition to 2.4s — which is the behavior we discussed. the kv cache hit rate climbs from 0 to 78% after the first window.
[10:25] Aisha Khan: hmm that tail is concerning, can you mitigate by using smaller shards?
[10:29] Evan Zhou: you can reduce kernel swap overhead by prepartitioning sequences or using model variants with long-kernel support; we also have a quantized variant that trades some quality for lower memory and smoother latency.
[10:44] Liam O'Connor: show us what happens when you ramp TPS while streaming is active.
[10:50] Evan Zhou: switching to the TPS dashboard and kicking a 1k to 4k qps ramp now.
[10:58] [demo] Console: as we ramp, queue depth spikes briefly but the warm pool absorbs most load; in hosted mode you see some routing to cheaper variants which increases 95th percentile slightly. in Dedicated mode with burst lanes we keep 95th under target.
[11:25] Tom Rivera: we also saw a case where slow clients caused backlog and then a few requests timed out with partial payloads; can you surface in logs when partial payloads are returned?
[11:35] Evan Zhou: yes, you can toggle verbose streaming logs; we tag partial payloads with a reason code (e.g., kernel_swap, mem_pressure) that shows up in the audit trail.
[11:52] [00:11:52] Aisha Khan: overall the demo looks good. what's the recommended POC scope?
[11:58] Maya Patel: propose a 4-week POC: week 1: benchmark harness and synthetic tests (long-context + TPS ramp); week 2: integrate sanitized real data + streaming UX tests; week 3: run production-like mixed traffic and iterate; week 4: review results and decide on Dedicated commit.
[12:18] Liam O'Connor: budget and timeline — procurement wants TCO and we need a decision by end of august.
[12:25] Maya Patel: we'll provide cost models for Hosted vs Dedicated and a recommended config for your expected loads; i'll send that in a follow-up.
[12:33] [00:12:33] Tom Rivera: for POC we'll need a security contact to review VPC configs.
[12:38] Maya Patel: assigning: i'll be the primary contact, and Evan will supply the network/architecture details.
[12:45] Aisha Khan: any gotchas with KMS integration? our key policies are strict.
[12:50] Evan Zhou: we support customer-managed KMS for Private and Dedicated; some hosted flows require additional attestation but we can walk through options.
[13:05] [00:13:05] Maya Patel: quick recap of artifacts to share: benchmark harness, pricing sheet, SOC2 + network diagrams, SDK snippets for streaming, and test plan.
[13:18] [00:13:18] Aisha Khan: great — please include recommended console settings for queue limits and token timeouts.
[13:24] Maya Patel: will do.
[13:28] [00:13:28] Liam O'Connor: last question — what happens if we want on-prem later? is migration path clear?
[13:33] Evan Zhou: yes, we support Private on VPC and on-prem packages; migration is mostly config and data movement with the same control plane APIs. we'll add migration docs to the repo link.
[13:50] [00:13:50] Maya Patel: ok everyone thanks — we'll follow up with the POC plan and the benchmark sheet. any other final questions?
[13:58] Aisha Khan: none from me, thanks.
[14:02] Tom Rivera: thanks team.
[14:05] Maya Patel: thanks all — next steps in the calendar and email.
